quiz.question: A product table uses status as the partition key, and almost every item is ACTIVE. Writes start throttling even though table-level capacity looks unused. What is the real problem?
quiz.optionA: DynamoDB cannot store more than one item per partition key
quiz.optionB: A low-cardinality partition key funnels traffic onto too few partitions (hot keys)
quiz.optionD: Sort keys are required for every write

quiz.question: Why do engineers treat the 400KB item size cap as a modeling constraint, not just a storage limit?
quiz.optionA: Larger items must be split across partitions automatically
quiz.optionB: Every read and write moves the whole item, so fat items amplify latency, cost, and hot-partition risk
quiz.optionC: Secondary indexes cannot project attributes under 400KB
quiz.optionD: Transactions fail if any item is under 400KB

quiz.question: A dashboard needs every order from last year with no known user or order id. Why is a table Scan usually the wrong first design?
quiz.optionA: Scan can only return one item
quiz.optionB: Scan walks the whole table, burns read capacity on irrelevant items, and gets slower as data grows
quiz.optionC: Scan is strongly consistent and therefore forbidden

quiz.question: When should you choose a strongly consistent read over the default eventually consistent read?
quiz.optionB: When the next decision cannot tolerate a replica that has not yet seen the latest write to that item
quiz.optionC: When reading from a global secondary index
quiz.optionD: When the item is larger than 400KB

quiz.question: On-demand vs provisioned capacity is mainly a statement about workload shape. Which pairing is right?
quiz.optionA: On-demand for spiky or unknown traffic; provisioned for steady, forecastable load
quiz.optionB: On-demand only for strongly consistent reads
quiz.optionC: Provisioned only for tables without sort keys

quiz.question: What does a well-chosen partition key actually control?
quiz.optionA: Which AWS region stores the table
quiz.optionB: How traffic is spread across storage partitions

quiz.question: You know userId and want that user's orders in a time range. Which operation matches the data model?
quiz.optionA: Scan with a filter on userId
quiz.optionB: Query on partition key userId and a sort-key condition on timestamp

quiz.question: A single celebrity userId receives a huge fraction of likes. Adaptive capacity cannot fully save you because:
quiz.optionA: All items for one partition key still share that key's throughput ceiling
quiz.optionB: DynamoDB forbids popular keys

quiz.question: Why store a profile photo URL (or S3 key) in DynamoDB instead of the image bytes?
quiz.optionA: URLs are the only string type DynamoDB allows
quiz.optionB: Images blow past the item-size model, make every user read heavier, and turn a metadata store into blob storage
quiz.optionD: Binary attributes are eventually consistent only

quiz.question: Filter expressions on a Scan or Query run after capacity is consumed. What does that imply?
quiz.optionA: Filters are a substitute for a good key design
quiz.optionB: You still pay to read items that the filter later throws away
quiz.optionC: Filters make the operation strongly consistent

quiz.question: Eventually consistent reads are the default because they:
quiz.optionB: Cost less and are enough when the client can tolerate a brief lag after a write
quiz.optionD: Are the only option for GetItem

quiz.question: A table has a sharp weekday peak and near-zero nights. What capacity shape fits without overpaying all week?
quiz.optionB: On-demand, or provisioned with auto scaling that tracks the daily curve
quiz.optionC: A global table in every region

quiz.question: What is the practical difference between GetItem and Query?
quiz.optionA: GetItem needs the full primary key for one item; Query reads a partition (optionally a sort-key range)
quiz.optionB: Query cannot use a sort key
quiz.optionD: They are identical if eventual consistency is on

quiz.question: High partition-key cardinality matters because:
quiz.optionB: Many distinct, relatively even keys let the service spread load; a handful of keys cannot

quiz.question: A GSI uses email as its partition key. Some emails are extremely popular write targets. What happens?
quiz.optionA: Only the base table can throttle; GSIs share infinite capacity
quiz.optionB: The GSI can hot-partition and backpressure base-table writes that must update that index

quiz.question: Why are GSI reads eventually consistent even if you request strong consistency on the table?
quiz.optionA: GSIs live in a separate replication path; they are not a strongly consistent projection of the base item
quiz.optionB: GSIs are stored on the client

quiz.question: You need to query users by status, but 95% of users are ACTIVE. Why is a GSI on status a poor partition design?
quiz.optionB: Status has almost no cardinality, so the ACTIVE partition becomes a hotspot

quiz.question: Each order item also updates two GSIs. Under a write-heavy workload this matters because:
quiz.optionB: Every base write fans out extra index writes, so write amplification and index hot keys become the limiter
quiz.optionC: GSIs batch all writes into one WCU
quiz.optionD: Index writes are free if the table is on-demand

quiz.question: A session blob is approaching a few hundred KB and is read on every API call. Best modeling move?
quiz.optionA: Keep growing the item; 400KB is a soft guideline
quiz.optionB: Move the blob to object storage and keep a pointer plus small, frequently read fields in DynamoDB
quiz.optionC: Store the blob as the partition key
quiz.optionD: Use Scan to fetch only one attribute

quiz.question: Provisioned capacity is set high at the table, but one partition key still throttles. What is the lesson?
quiz.optionA: Table-level capacity is not a guarantee for a single hot key
quiz.optionB: Throttling always means the account is out of quota

quiz.question: Sparse GSIs (only items that have the index keys) are useful because:
quiz.optionA: They make every item strongly consistent
quiz.optionB: They keep the index small and aligned to a real access path instead of indexing the whole table

quiz.question: Write sharding (userId#0 .. userId#N) helps a hot key. What cost do you accept?
quiz.optionB: Reads that need the full picture must fan in across shards, and shard count becomes part of the model

quiz.question: A reporting job Scans nightly 'because it is off-peak'. Why can this still hurt production?
quiz.optionB: Scan still consumes read capacity and can steal throughput from live partitions if not isolated (separate table/export/on-demand job design)
quiz.optionC: Scans convert the table to provisioned

quiz.question: You need 'read my write' on the same item in one request path. Which read should you use?
quiz.optionA: Eventually consistent GetItem on a GSI
quiz.optionB: Strongly consistent GetItem/Query on the base table

quiz.question: Steady 5k QPS all day vs a flash-sale spike to 80k for 20 minutes. Capacity modes?
quiz.optionB: Steady load often fits provisioned; the flash-sale shape is why on-demand (or a big scale-up plan) exists
quiz.optionD: Provisioned ignores partition keys during spikes

quiz.question: Projecting ALL attributes into a GSI is convenient. The downside is:
quiz.optionB: Index storage and write cost track the full item, so fat items make the GSI expensive and slower to update
quiz.optionC: You can no longer Query the GSI

quiz.question: A Query without a partition key is invalid because:
quiz.optionA: Query is just a slower Scan
quiz.optionB: Query is defined as 'read this partition (and maybe a sort-key slice)', not 'search the table'
quiz.optionC: Partition keys are optional on tables

quiz.question: Condition checks (optimistic locking with a version attribute) exist because:
quiz.optionB: Two writers can overwrite the same item; you need a predicate so the second write fails instead of clobbering
quiz.optionD: Strongly consistent reads lock the item

quiz.question: Adaptive capacity moved extra throughput toward a hot partition, but p99 still collapses on one productId. What is left?
quiz.optionB: Change the key (shard, invert access pattern, or cache) because one key is a physical bottleneck

quiz.question: A leaderboard GSI partition key is the constant LEADERBOARD. Why will this fail at scale?
quiz.optionA: Constants are not valid attribute names
quiz.optionB: Every write lands on one index partition; you modeled a global hot key

quiz.question: Single-table design is not 'put everything in one table'. The actual rule is:
quiz.optionA: Minimize the number of AWS resources on the bill
quiz.optionB: Shape items and keys so each access pattern is a Query on a partition, not a Scan across entity types
quiz.optionD: Store blobs inline to avoid joins

quiz.question: A 350KB item is updated 20 times a second to flip one flag. Why is this an incident waiting to happen?
quiz.optionB: Each update rewrites the whole large item, multiplying write cost and making that key hotter than the business change requires

quiz.question: You need atomic debit of account A and credit of account B. Why is 'two PutItems' insufficient?
quiz.optionB: Each item write is atomic alone; a crash between them can strand money unless you use a transaction or a modeled workflow
quiz.optionC: Accounts must share a partition key always
quiz.optionD: Strongly consistent reads provide atomic multi-item writes

quiz.question: Global tables give you multi-region copies. What do they not give you?
quiz.optionA: Lower read latency near a replica
quiz.optionB: A single globally strongly consistent item view for every read
quiz.optionC: Regional isolation if you design for it
quiz.optionD: The same partition-key model in each region

quiz.question: A GSI is KEYS_ONLY. A query against it still needs five large attributes. Tradeoff?
quiz.optionA: The GSI returns those attributes for free
quiz.optionB: You do a cheap index Query then GetItem the base rows; you avoided write amplification at the cost of extra reads
quiz.optionD: You must Scan the base table

quiz.question: Time-series data with PK = today's date concentrates today's writes. A better key shape is:
quiz.optionB: Shard by a high-cardinality id (device, customer, or time bucket + shard) so ingests spread, and query by the access pattern you actually have
quiz.optionD: No partition key, sort key only

quiz.question: On-demand still throttles a partition. Why are people surprised?
quiz.optionB: On-demand removes table-level provisioning, not the physics of a single hot key or a sudden jump beyond what that partition can absorb

quiz.question: Exporting to S3 / using an incremental export for analytics is preferred over a live Scan because:
quiz.optionB: You isolate heavy read traffic from the online table's partitions and capacity

quiz.question: A cache in front of DynamoDB for a hot product key helps reads. What must you still design for?
quiz.optionA: The cache makes writes strongly consistent across regions
quiz.optionB: Cache misses, TTL expiry, and stampede can slam the same hot key; writes still hit DynamoDB
quiz.optionC: Partition keys are no longer needed

quiz.question: Why model 1:N as partition key = parent and sort key = child rather than embedding an unbounded list on the parent?
quiz.optionA: Lists are not a DynamoDB type
quiz.optionB: The parent item would grow toward 400KB, every child change would rewrite the parent, and you could not Query a slice of children

quiz.question: Strongly consistent reads cost more and still do not make a GSI or a global-table replica 'the truth everywhere'. The honest contract is:
quiz.optionA: Strong reads are a quorum read of that table's item in that region, not a global lock
quiz.optionB: Strong reads lock all GSIs
quiz.optionC: Strong reads are free on on-demand

quiz.question: You are asked to 'just add an index' for an unplanned access pattern. What do you check first?
quiz.optionA: Whether the new key has cardinality and even traffic, and whether the extra write fan-out is acceptable
quiz.optionB: Whether Scan would be faster
quiz.optionD: Whether the index can be strongly consistent

quiz.question: Redis executes commands on a primary single thread (per process). A slow KEYS or huge SUNION therefore:
quiz.optionB: Blocks other clients on that instance until it finishes

quiz.question: Why is Redis a cache or speed layer, not the system of record, in most architectures?
quiz.optionB: Memory, eviction, async replicas, and restart/restore behavior mean data can disappear; durable truth belongs in a database designed for it

quiz.question: RDB vs AOF in one line:
quiz.optionA: RDB is a point-in-time snapshot; AOF logs writes for a tighter durability window, at more I/O cost
quiz.optionB: AOF is only for cluster slots

quiz.question: maxmemory is hit and the policy is allkeys-lru. What happens to a new SET?
quiz.optionB: Redis evicts some existing key to free memory, then accepts the write
quiz.optionC: Redis spills to disk as the source of truth

quiz.question: A cache stampede (thundering herd) is:
quiz.optionA: AOF rewrite using too many cores
quiz.optionB: Many clients missing the same expired key at once and all hitting the database together

quiz.question: In Redis Cluster, a key maps to a hash slot. Multi-key commands work only when:
quiz.optionA: All keys live in the same slot (often forced with a hash tag)
quiz.optionB: You use KEYS first

quiz.question: KEYS * in production is dangerous because:
quiz.optionB: It is a blocking, whole-keyspace scan on a single-threaded server

quiz.question: TTL on a cache key means:
quiz.optionB: Redis may drop the key after expiry; the source of truth must still exist elsewhere if you need it
quiz.optionC: The key is persisted to RDB immediately

quiz.question: Pipelining helps throughput because:
quiz.optionB: The client sends many commands without waiting for each round trip, feeding the single-threaded loop more work per RTT

quiz.question: noeviction as a maxmemory policy means:
quiz.optionB: Writes that need memory fail instead of dropping other keys
quiz.optionC: Redis becomes the source of truth

quiz.question: Reading from a replica can be stale because:
quiz.optionB: Replication is asynchronous; a write on the primary may not have arrived yet

quiz.question: A huge value on one hot key is a problem even with Cluster because:
quiz.optionB: That key still lives on one node and is served by one command loop; Cluster shards keys, not a single giant value

quiz.question: If the process restarts and you only have occasional RDB snapshots, you should expect:
quiz.optionB: Loss of writes since the last snapshot unless AOF (or a real database) covers them

quiz.question: volatile-lru evicts:
quiz.optionB: Only keys that already have an expire set

quiz.question: A Lua script in Redis is attractive for compare-and-set because:
quiz.optionA: Lua runs on all cluster nodes as a distributed transaction
quiz.optionB: The script runs atomically on that instance's single thread, so no other command interleaves
quiz.optionD: Lua is persisted as the source of truth

quiz.question: AOF fsync every second vs always: the product question is:
quiz.optionB: How much acknowledged write loss you accept on a crash versus how hard you hit the disk

quiz.question: Cache stampede mitigation that belongs in the app, not just a longer TTL:
quiz.optionB: Single-flight / mutex per key, probabilistic early expiry, or serving stale while one worker refills
quiz.optionD: Store everything without TTLs and never evict

quiz.question: Hash tags like {user:42}:profile and {user:42}:orders exist so that:
quiz.optionB: Both keys hash to the same cluster slot and can be used in one multi-key command
quiz.optionC: AOF groups them into one fsync
quiz.optionD: They become the database of record

quiz.question: MULTI/EXEC is not a distributed transaction. It:
quiz.optionB: Queues commands and runs them sequentially on one instance; Cluster still will not span slots

quiz.question: A background RDB save (fork) on a huge dataset can stall latency because:
quiz.optionB: Copy-on-write after fork can spike memory and pause the process under write load

quiz.question: You treat Redis lists as a job queue and crash the worker after LPOP. What did you lose?
quiz.optionA: Nothing; AOF always replays the job to the worker
quiz.optionB: The job, unless you used a reliable pattern (BRPOPLPUSH/streams + ack) and a real backing store for truth

quiz.question: Hot key on one cluster node shows 100% CPU while others are idle. Fix is not 'add replicas of other nodes' but:
quiz.optionB: Split the key (sharding in the app), cache locally, or read-fanout carefully; the slot/node owning that key is the bottleneck

quiz.question: allkeys-lfu vs allkeys-lru: you pick LFU when:
quiz.optionB: Frequency beats recency: a key read often should survive even if it was not the most recently touched

quiz.question: Pub/Sub is a poor audit log because:
quiz.optionB: It is fire-and-forget in-memory fanout; disconnected subscribers miss messages and nothing is the source of truth
quiz.optionC: It uses too many cluster slots

quiz.question: A connection pool of 5000 clients against one instance can still collapse throughput because:
quiz.optionA: Redis only allows one TCP connection
quiz.optionB: The single thread plus huge output buffers and context switching become the limit; more conns are not more cores

quiz.question: SCAN is preferred over KEYS because:
quiz.optionA: SCAN is strongly consistent across the cluster
quiz.optionB: It incrementally iterates without holding the server in one giant blocking call
quiz.optionD: SCAN never misses keys even if they are mutated

quiz.question: If eviction is on, a successful SET is not a durability guarantee. Why?
quiz.optionB: The key can still be dropped later under memory pressure, and a crash can lose recent writes depending on RDB/AOF settings
quiz.optionD: TTL is ignored when eviction is on

quiz.question: Using Redis as a distributed lock without a well-tested algorithm is risky because:
quiz.optionB: Expiry, pauses, and failover can leave two clients thinking they hold the lock; Redis is not a consensus database
quiz.optionC: Cluster slots cannot store lock keys

quiz.question: A cluster slot migration is in progress. Clients must handle:
quiz.optionA: A frozen keyspace with no errors
quiz.optionB: ASK/MOVED redirects and transient multi-key failures; treating Redis like a single always-local node will break
quiz.optionD: Synchronous replica promotion of every key

quiz.question: WAIT or WAITAOF after a write is how you:
quiz.optionA: Make Redis a multi-primary consensus store
quiz.optionB: Block until replicas (or AOF) catch up to a durability bar you chose; default writes do not wait

quiz.question: Big keys (a million-member hash) hurt more than memory size because:
quiz.optionB: Many commands become O(N) on the single thread (serialize, expire, replica sync, client output)

quiz.question: Stampede plus a single-threaded Redis plus a slow DB fill is a cascade. A robust refill looks like:
quiz.optionB: One owner refills, others wait or serve stale; optionally jitter TTLs; never let N app servers all reconstruct the same key

quiz.question: Why still persist a write to Postgres (or similar) when Redis already SET it?
quiz.optionB: Redis may evict, lose a replica, or replay an older RDB; the database is the source of truth, Redis is a copy
quiz.optionD: AOF cannot store the same string

quiz.question: Client-side caching / tracking exists because:
quiz.optionA: The server thread wants more KEYS calls
quiz.optionB: Even an in-memory round trip is expensive at huge QPS; local memory with invalidation beats a hot Redis key

quiz.question: AOF rewrite and RDB fork at the same time on a memory-tight host. Operational risk?
quiz.optionB: Double copy-on-write memory spike, latency stall, or OOM killer — persistence settings are a capacity plan, not just 'on'

quiz.question: Streams with consumer groups beat a naive list queue when:
quiz.optionB: You need pending entries, acknowledgements, and replay after a worker crash — still not a durable business ledger by itself
quiz.optionD: You want eviction to delete jobs first

quiz.question: Hash-slot coverage after a node death: the cluster goes down for those slots unless:
quiz.optionB: Replicas exist for that node and failover succeeds; Redis Cluster is not magic extra durability of the data model

quiz.question: A 'Redis transaction' across keys in different slots needs:
quiz.optionB: A different design: hash tags to colocate, an external workflow, or a real database transaction — Cluster will refuse the cross-slot MULTI

quiz.question: Blocking commands (BLPOP, BZPOPMIN) on a shared instance interact with the single thread how?
quiz.optionA: They run on a second GIL
quiz.optionB: They park that client, but a flood of them plus large fanout still competes for the one command loop and output buffers

quiz.question: You observe p99 spikes every N minutes with no app deploy. A likely Redis cause is:
quiz.optionB: Fork-based persistence, large expiry storms, or big-key commands — all block or stall the same thread

quiz.question: Serving cache-aside correctly means on write you:
quiz.optionA: Only SET Redis and trust eviction to notify the DB
quiz.optionB: Write the database first (or in a defined order) and invalidate/update Redis so the cache cannot resurrect stale truth
quiz.optionD: Disable TTL so Redis becomes source of truth

quiz.question: Why can pipelining + Cluster be wrong if you blindly batch keys?
quiz.optionB: A pipeline is still per-node; mixed slots must be split by slot or you get CROSSSLOT / extra hops
quiz.optionD: Pipelines disable eviction mid-batch as a transaction

quiz.question: S3 is the wrong place to implement 'query users where lastLogin > X' because:
quiz.optionB: It is an object store: get-by-key, not a query engine with secondary indexes and predicates
quiz.optionC: S3 deletes data after one day

quiz.question: Durability of an object is achieved by:
quiz.optionA: A published SLA number you should memorize as the design
quiz.optionB: Storing multiple copies and verifying checksums so bit rot and disk loss do not silently win
quiz.optionC: Keeping one copy in the client's browser

quiz.question: Millions of tiny files (few KB each) get expensive and slow mainly because:
quiz.optionB: You pay per request and listing/metadata work dominates; throughput is not 'one disk sequential read'

quiz.question: Old-style keys like 2024-01-01/log1, 2024-01-01/log2 created prefix hotspots because:
quiz.optionB: Many clients hammered the same key prefix/partition at once instead of spreading request load

quiz.question: SQS standard queues are at-least-once. Your consumer must:
quiz.optionA: Assume each message is processed exactly one time
quiz.optionB: Be idempotent; the same message can be delivered more than once
quiz.optionC: Use S3 listing as the lock

quiz.question: Updating a 'row' in S3 means:
quiz.optionA: A SQL UPDATE of one field
quiz.optionB: Replace the whole object (or write a new version); there is no in-place field update
quiz.optionC: A strongly consistent multi-object transaction by default

quiz.question: Visibility timeout on SQS exists so that:
quiz.optionA: Messages become source of truth in S3
quiz.optionB: Other consumers hide the message while one works; if you crash, it reappears (at-least-once)

quiz.question: Putting a database dump on S3 is backup. Using S3 as the live order table is wrong because:
quiz.optionB: You lack cheap conditional updates, queries, and low-latency item access as a primary OLTP store

quiz.question: A PUT of a new object should include integrity protection by:
quiz.optionB: Sending a checksum and verifying it on read; copies plus checksums are the durability story
quiz.optionD: Storing only in one AZ in the app

quiz.question: Listing a bucket with millions of keys as your 'index' is a bad database because:
quiz.optionB: List is paginated, costly, and not a query planner; you needed a real index or a manifest object

quiz.question: SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues is useful when:
quiz.optionA: You need exactly-once across all consumers without idempotency
quiz.optionB: Several independent workers should each see the event; each queue still delivers at-least-once

quiz.question: Small-file problem on S3 is often fixed by:
quiz.optionB: Batching many logical records into larger objects (and maybe a real database for metadata)

quiz.question: S3 read-after-write for new objects is strongly consistent now. That still does not make S3 a database because:
quiz.optionA: Consistency was the only missing SQL feature
quiz.optionB: You still have no rich queries, joins, or cheap partial updates — only object I/O

quiz.question: Why spread entropy in the key (or a hash prefix) for high QPS ingest?
quiz.optionB: To avoid concentrating request rate on one logical prefix as the workload scales

quiz.question: A Lambda processes SQS and writes S3. The Lambda times out after the PUT but before delete. What happens?
quiz.optionB: The message returns after visibility timeout; you may PUT again — object writes and queue acks need idempotency keys

quiz.question: S3 Select / Glacier select still does not replace a warehouse when:
quiz.optionB: You need repeated ad-hoc joins, mutating indexes, and concurrent transactional updates

quiz.question: Versioning helps durability and recovery. It does not help you if:
quiz.optionA: You overwrite by mistake and want the old bytes
quiz.optionB: You needed a queryable current-row store; versions are extra objects, not an OLTP log you can SQL
quiz.optionD: You want to retrieve a prior checksummed copy

quiz.question: Request costs for 1 billion 1KB objects vs one 1GB object differ because:
quiz.optionB: PUT/GET/LIST are billed per request; tiny objects turn storage into an API-tax problem

quiz.question: FIFO SQS gives ordering per message group and exactly-once processing attempts inside a window, but you still:
quiz.optionB: Design consumers for retries, replays, and downstream side effects that may run more than once

quiz.question: A data lake on S3 plus Athena/Spark works when the object layout is:
quiz.optionA: One tiny file per event in a single hot prefix
quiz.optionB: Partitioned, reasonably sized files (columnar) so listing and scan costs stay bounded

quiz.question: Multipart upload is for large objects. Incomplete parts become a cost leak unless you:
quiz.optionB: Abort abandoned uploads and set a lifecycle rule on incomplete parts

quiz.question: If-Match / If-None-Match on S3 give you optimistic concurrency for one key. They do not give you:
quiz.optionA: A way to avoid clobbering a single object
quiz.optionB: Multi-key transactions like a database

quiz.question: CloudFront in front of S3 helps popular reads. Origin load still spikes when:
quiz.optionB: Cache misses, low TTL, or a unique-key stampede all go to the same prefix/object

quiz.question: Storing session state only in S3 for a low-latency API is usually wrong because:
quiz.optionB: Object GET/PUT latency and no cheap mutate path lose to an in-memory or purpose-built session store

quiz.question: S3 Event Notifications to SQS can fire more than once for the same object change. Downstream must:
quiz.optionA: Treat notifications as exactly-once ledger entries
quiz.optionB: Dedupe on object key + version/etag and stay idempotent

quiz.question: Lifecycle transitions to colder storage classes are about access shape. A bad fit is:
quiz.optionB: Objects you mutate or read with tight latency all day — retrieval cost and delay dominate

quiz.question: A 'manifest.json' object listing parts is a common S3 pattern because:
quiz.optionA: S3 cannot store more than one object
quiz.optionB: The bucket is not an index; you explicitly store the catalog you would have queried in a database

quiz.question: DLQs exist on SQS because at-least-once plus poison messages would otherwise:
quiz.optionB: Retry forever, blocking the queue; you isolate failures without pretending delivery was exactly-once

quiz.question: Cross-region replication of S3 objects is asynchronous. Designing a 'read in region B immediately after write in A' as if it were a commit is wrong because:
quiz.optionB: Replication lag means B may not have the object yet; it is not a distributed database transaction
quiz.optionD: SQS becomes exactly-once when CRR is on

quiz.question: You need append-only analytics events. Why not one S3 PUT per click from the browser?
quiz.optionA: S3 cannot be written from the internet with the right IAM
quiz.optionB: Tiny-object request cost, prefix hotspots, and no server-side aggregation; buffer in Kinesis/SQS/Firehose then write large objects
quiz.optionD: At-least-once queues forbid this path only

quiz.question: Compare-and-swap with ETags on a hot inventory object serializes the world onto one key. At scale you:
quiz.optionB: Shard the object, use a real database for the hot row, or accept queue-based serialization — S3 is not a write-optimized row store
quiz.optionC: Turn off checksums to go faster
quiz.optionD: Use sequential date prefixes for inventory

quiz.question: A pipeline is 'SQS -> worker -> S3 -> notify next queue'. End-to-end exactly-once is:
quiz.optionB: Not given; each hop is at-least-once, so idempotent writes (keyed objects/versions) are the real contract

quiz.question: S3 Object Lock / WORM helps compliance. Using it as a queue ack store is a smell because:
quiz.optionB: You wanted a messaging semantic (visibility, retry, DLQ), not immutability of blobs

quiz.question: Inventory reports and S3 Batch exist because listing the live bucket as a control plane:
quiz.optionA: Is a strongly consistent SQL view
quiz.optionB: Does not scale as a database catalog; you snapshot metadata out of band

quiz.question: A KMS-encrypted bucket plus many tiny GETs is slow/expensive because:
quiz.optionB: Each request can add KMS authz/decrypt overhead on top of the small-file request tax

quiz.question: You replicated objects and now readers see old and new writers. The durable copies did their job; the missing piece is:
quiz.optionB: An application-level version/epoch so readers know which object generation is authoritative

quiz.question: Using S3 as a lockfile (PUT if not exists, then work) fails under contention because:
quiz.optionB: There is no robust lease/fencing story like a consensus lock; timeouts and retries produce split brain

quiz.question: Firehose/Kinesis rolling files into S3 every N MB or N seconds is about:
quiz.optionB: Turning a high-QPS small-event stream into large, checksummed objects with spread prefixes

quiz.question: A consumer 'succeeds' if it PUTs to S3 but crashes before finishing side effects. Replay will PUT again. The object key should be:
quiz.optionA: A random UUID every attempt so nothing clashes
quiz.optionB: Deterministic from the message id / business id so retries overwrite the same checksummed object
quiz.optionC: The current timestamp to the nanosecond

quiz.question: Strongly consistent GET of a key is not isolation for a multi-step workflow because:
quiz.optionB: Two objects (or object + queue + table) are not one transaction; you compose idempotent steps
quiz.optionD: SQS FIFO wraps S3 in a transaction

quiz.question: Hot prefix plus small files plus a LIST-heavy UI is a triple hit. The architecture move is:
quiz.optionB: Metadata in a database or index, objects in S3 with hashed prefixes and batched file sizes; never LIST as the product query

quiz.question: Durability of copies does not protect you from a bad DELETE in the app. You still need:
quiz.optionB: Versioning, MFA-delete/Object Lock, IAM least privilege, and backups — operational mistakes are not disk failures
quiz.optionC: At-most-once SQS so deletes never retry

flashcards.question: What is a hot key?
flashcards.answer: A partition key (or key range) that receives a disproportionate share of reads/writes so one partition throttles while the table still looks like it has spare capacity.

flashcards.question: Why does partition-key cardinality matter?
flashcards.answer: DynamoDB spreads load by key. Low-cardinality keys (status=ACTIVE) collapse traffic onto few partitions; high, even cardinality lets the table scale.

flashcards.question: Why do Scans hurt as the table grows?
flashcards.answer: Scan reads every item (you still pay for filtered-out rows), eats read capacity, and latency tracks table size. Prefer Query on keys that match an access pattern.

flashcards.question: How should you model around the 400KB item limit?
flashcards.answer: Keep items metadata-sized. Put large blobs in object storage and store a pointer. Split 1:N into item collections (PK=parent, SK=child) instead of a giant nested list.

flashcards.question: Strongly consistent vs eventually consistent reads?
flashcards.answer: Eventual is cheaper and fine if a brief lag is OK. Strong (base table only) is for read-my-write on that item in that region. GSIs are eventual.

flashcards.question: On-demand vs provisioned as workload shape?
flashcards.answer: On-demand fits spiky/unknown traffic. Provisioned (often with autoscaling) fits steady, forecastable QPS. Neither removes a single hot key.

flashcards.question: Query vs GetItem vs Scan?
flashcards.answer: GetItem: one item by full primary key. Query: one partition, optional sort-key range. Scan: whole table — last resort, not an access pattern.

flashcards.question: What does the partition key actually choose?
flashcards.answer: Which partition stores the item and therefore where that item's throughput is accounted. Design keys from access patterns, not from ER diagrams.

flashcards.question: How can a GSI take down base-table writes?
flashcards.answer: Each base write that touches indexed attributes must update the GSI. A hot or throttled GSI partition backpressures those writes. Indexes have their own heat.

flashcards.question: GSI limits you should recite in an interview?
flashcards.answer: GSIs are eventually consistent, add write amplification, need their own capacity/heat planning, and a low-cardinality GSI PK is as bad as a low-cardinality table PK.

flashcards.question: What is a sparse GSI for?
flashcards.answer: Only items that have the index attributes appear. You get a small index aligned to a rare access path instead of projecting the entire table.

flashcards.question: Write sharding for a hot key: how and what is the cost?
flashcards.answer: Append a shard id to the PK so writes spread. Readers fan in across shards. Shard count becomes part of the contract.

flashcards.question: Why aren't filter expressions a substitute for keys?
flashcards.answer: Capacity is consumed before the filter. You still read (and pay for) items you throw away. Filters refine a Query; they do not create an access pattern.

flashcards.question: KEYS_ONLY vs ALL projections?
flashcards.answer: KEYS_ONLY keeps index writes small; you GetItem the base row after. ALL makes the GSI a fat copy — convenient reads, expensive writes as items grow.

flashcards.question: When do you actually need a strongly consistent read?
flashcards.answer: When the next decision cannot accept a replica lag on that base-table item (read-your-write, balance check). Not 'always', and not on GSIs.

flashcards.question: Table-level capacity looked fine but one key throttled. Lesson?
flashcards.answer: Throughput is not a shared buffet for every key. Provisioned/on-demand numbers are not a per-key SLA. Fix the key or cache/shard it.

flashcards.question: Why can't adaptive capacity save a celebrity key?
flashcards.answer: It can shift spare throughput toward a busy partition, but one partition key is still one bottleneck. Popular item => shard, cache, or change the pattern.

flashcards.question: Why not embed an unbounded child list on the parent item?
flashcards.answer: The parent races toward 400KB, every child write rewrites the fat item, and you cannot Query a slice. Model children as SK range under the parent PK.

flashcards.question: What does a DynamoDB transaction buy you — and not buy you?
flashcards.answer: Atomic all-or-nothing across a small set of items in a region. Not global linearizability, not unbounded size, not a substitute for good keys.

flashcards.question: Single-table design in one sentence?
flashcards.answer: Precompute access paths into item collections you can Query; not 'one table to save money' and not an excuse to Scan entity types together.

flashcards.question: Time-series PK = today's date: why is it a hotspot?
flashcards.answer: All of today's ingest hits one key. Shard by device/customer/time-bucket+shard so writes spread; do not concentrate 'now' on a single PK.

flashcards.question: Global tables vs strongly consistent reads?
flashcards.answer: Strong read is a regional guarantee on the base item. Global tables replicate asynchronously across regions — not one worldwide strongly consistent copy.

flashcards.question: Cache in front of a hot DynamoDB key: remaining risks?
flashcards.answer: Misses, TTL expiry, and stampedes refocus load on the same key. Writes still hit DynamoDB. Cache is a read valve, not a new partition key.

flashcards.question: Analytics via live Scan vs export?
flashcards.answer: Export/offline pipeline isolates heavy reads from online partitions. A 'nightly Scan' still competes for the same capacity and can starve production.

flashcards.question: What does Redis's single-threaded command loop imply?
flashcards.answer: One slow or O(N) command blocks other clients on that process. More connections ≠ more cores. Avoid KEYS, huge values, and heavy aggregates on the hot instance.

flashcards.question: Why is Redis not the source of truth?
flashcards.answer: Memory + eviction + async replicas + snapshot/AOF gaps mean data can vanish. Persist business state in a database; Redis holds a speed copy.

flashcards.question: RDB vs AOF?
flashcards.answer: RDB: compact point-in-time snapshot, more potential loss since last save. AOF: logs writes for a tighter durability window, more disk work. Often combined.

flashcards.question: What is eviction?
flashcards.answer: When maxmemory is hit, Redis drops keys by policy (allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, LFU, noeviction, …). A SET can succeed now and still disappear later.

flashcards.question: What is a cache stampede?
flashcards.answer: Many clients miss the same expired/hot key at once and all hit the origin. Mitigate with single-flight, stale-while-revalidate, and jittered TTLs.

flashcards.question: What are cluster slots?
flashcards.answer: The keyspace is split into hash slots owned by nodes. A key lives in one slot. Multi-key ops need the same slot (hash tags like {userId}).

flashcards.question: KEYS vs SCAN?
flashcards.answer: KEYS * blocks the single thread over the whole keyspace. SCAN iterates incrementally and is the production-safe way to walk keys.

flashcards.question: What does a TTL actually guarantee?
flashcards.answer: The cache entry may go away. It is not a business delete in the source of truth and not a durability mechanism.

flashcards.question: Why Lua scripts for compare-and-set?
flashcards.answer: The script runs atomically on that instance's thread — no other command interleaves. It is not a cluster-wide transaction across slots.

flashcards.question: AOF fsync always vs every second?
flashcards.answer: Always: less loss, more disk latency. Every second: you may lose about a second of acknowledged writes on crash. Durability is a chosen budget.

flashcards.question: What are hash tags for?
flashcards.answer: {shared} prefixes force keys into the same cluster slot so MULTI/MGET/Lua can run. Over-tagging recreates a hot node.

flashcards.question: Why can RDB fork stall a huge instance?
flashcards.answer: Fork + copy-on-write under writes spikes memory and can pause the process. Persistence is part of the capacity plan.

flashcards.question: List as a queue: what do you lose on LPOP + crash?
flashcards.answer: The job is gone from Redis. Use streams/consumer groups or BRPOPLPUSH-style patterns, and still keep durable truth elsewhere.

flashcards.question: Hot key in Cluster: why don't extra nodes help?
flashcards.answer: One key maps to one slot on one primary. Idle nodes cannot serve that key. Split the key, cache locally, or change the model.

flashcards.question: Why is Pub/Sub a bad audit log?
flashcards.answer: Fire-and-forget in-memory fanout. If you were disconnected, you missed it. No durable source of truth.

flashcards.question: noeviction vs allkeys-lru for a cache?
flashcards.answer: Cache: usually an LRU/LFU policy so the process keeps serving. noeviction makes writes fail when memory is full — better for data you must not drop, but then Redis is a poor fit as the only store.

flashcards.question: What must Cluster clients handle during slot migration?
flashcards.answer: MOVED/ASK redirects and transient cross-slot errors. A pipeline of mixed-slot keys is not one node-local batch.

flashcards.question: WAIT / WAITAOF after a write?
flashcards.answer: Optional barrier until replicas or AOF meet a durability bar. Default SET does not wait. Still not full consensus like a database commit.

flashcards.question: Why are big keys worse than 'they use RAM'?
flashcards.answer: Serialization, expiry, replica sync, and many commands become O(N) on the single thread. Split hashes/lists/streams.

flashcards.question: Correct cache-aside write path?
flashcards.answer: Write the database, then invalidate (or carefully update) Redis so a stale cache cannot resurrect old truth. Do not treat SET as commit.

flashcards.question: Stampede + single thread + slow DB fill?
flashcards.answer: One owner refills; others wait or serve stale; jitter TTLs. Never let N app servers reconstruct the same key at once into one Redis thread.

flashcards.question: Streams/consumer groups vs 'Redis is my job system of record'?
flashcards.answer: Groups give pending lists and acks after worker crash. Useful. Still memory/eviction/persistence limited — not your financial ledger.

flashcards.question: Node death in Cluster?
flashcards.answer: Slots on that node are unavailable until a replica fails over. No replica => those keys are gone from the cluster until restore. Plan replicas.

flashcards.question: Cross-slot MULTI/EXEC?
flashcards.answer: Refused. Colocate with hash tags, or use an external workflow/database transaction. Redis 'transactions' are one-instance command queues.

flashcards.question: Why is S3 not a database?
flashcards.answer: It stores objects addressed by key. No secondary indexes, joins, or cheap field updates. GET/PUT/LIST are not SQL.

flashcards.question: How does S3 durability actually work?
flashcards.answer: Multiple copies plus checksums to detect corruption. Design around copies and integrity checks, not around reciting an SLA percentage.

flashcards.question: What is a prefix hotspot?
flashcards.answer: A burst of requests concentrated on one key prefix (classic sequential dates). Spread entropy in keys so request rate is not pinned to one partition.

flashcards.question: Why are tiny files expensive on S3?
flashcards.answer: Per-request and listing costs dominate storage. Batch records into larger objects; keep metadata in a real index if you must query.

flashcards.question: What does at-least-once SQS require of you?
flashcards.answer: Idempotent consumers. The same message can be delivered twice after a timeout, crash, or retry.

flashcards.question: How do you 'update a row' in S3?
flashcards.answer: Write a new object (or version) of the whole blob. There is no in-place column update.

flashcards.question: What is visibility timeout?
flashcards.answer: The hide window while a consumer works. Crash before delete => message reappears. That is at-least-once, not a lost-work bug in SQS.

flashcards.question: Why not LIST a million-key bucket as your product index?
flashcards.answer: LIST is paginated, costly, and not a query planner. Store a catalog (DB or manifest object) and treat S3 as the blob store.

flashcards.question: Lambda PUT to S3 then timeout before SQS delete — what must be true?
flashcards.answer: Replay will happen. Object keys and side effects must be idempotent (deterministic keys, version ids, upserts).

flashcards.question: S3 ETag / If-Match gives you what — and not what?
flashcards.answer: Optimistic concurrency on one key. Not multi-object transactions, not a row store, not a lock service.

flashcards.question: Why batch events into columnar files for a data lake?
flashcards.answer: Analytics engines want reasonably sized files and partitions. One-tiny-file-per-event explodes LIST/GET cost and planning time.

flashcards.question: FIFO SQS vs skipping idempotency?
flashcards.answer: FIFO orders a group and dedupes in a window. Downstream side effects can still run twice. Design retries on purpose.

flashcards.question: S3 event notifications can duplicate. What do you dedupe on?
flashcards.answer: Object key plus version/etag (or a business event id). Treat notifications like at-least-once queue messages.

flashcards.question: When are cold storage classes a bad fit?
flashcards.answer: When objects are read or overwritten with tight latency. Retrieval delay and cost dominate; keep hot data on a hot class or a database.

flashcards.question: Why a manifest object?
flashcards.answer: The bucket is not an index. You explicitly store the list of parts/files you would have queried if this were a database.

flashcards.question: What is a DLQ for?
flashcards.answer: Poison messages that fail repeatedly. Isolate them instead of blocking the queue or pretending delivery was exactly-once.

flashcards.question: Is cross-region replication a commit?
flashcards.answer: No. It is async. Region B may not have the object yet. Not a multi-region database transaction.

flashcards.question: Browser PUT per click to S3 — why not?
flashcards.answer: Tiny-object tax, prefix heat, no aggregation. Buffer in a stream/Firehose/queue, then roll large checksummed objects.

flashcards.question: CAS on one hot S3 inventory object?
flashcards.answer: Serializes the world onto a blob store key. Shard, use a database for the hot row, or queue the writes.

flashcards.question: End-to-end exactly-once through SQS and S3?
flashcards.answer: You don't get it. Each hop is at-least-once. Idempotent, deterministic object keys are the contract.

flashcards.question: S3 as a lockfile — why does it split-brain?
flashcards.answer: No robust lease/fencing. Timeouts and retries let two workers both believe they hold the lock. Use a real lock/consensus service.

flashcards.question: Deterministic object keys on retry — why?
flashcards.answer: If the consumer PUTs then crashes before ack, replay should overwrite the same key, not create duplicate random objects.

flashcards.question: Strong GET of one key vs workflow isolation?
flashcards.answer: One object read is not a transaction across object + queue + table. Compose idempotent steps with explicit versions.

flashcards.question: Copies protect disks, not DELETE in the app. Then what?
flashcards.answer: Versioning, Object Lock/MFA-delete, tight IAM, and backups. Operational deletes are not the same failure mode as bit rot.
